essay:
Every music nerd knows the Village in 1961 — Dylan arriving in the snow at Café Wha?, the folk boom, the hootenannies. Almost none of them know the woman Dylan himself called his favorite singer in the place. Karen Dalton (1937-1993) was the Cherokee-blooded blues singer from Enid, Oklahoma who showed up in Greenwich Village with a 12-string guitar, a long-neck banjo, one of her two kids, and two missing bottom teeth. She refused to sing her own songs, loathed recording, and cut only two albums in her life — each a small miracle that required being tricked into the studio. She died broke in a mobile home outside Woodstock in 1993 of an AIDS-related illness, age 55. Then, like a lot of the best ghosts, she came back.

Bob Dylan, Chronicles Volume One (p.12): "My favorite singer in the place was Karen Dalton — She was a tall white blues singer and guitar player, funky, lanky, and sultry. I'd actually met her before, run across her the previous summer outside Denver in a mountain pass town in a folk club. Karen had a voice like Billie Holiday's and played the guitar like Jimmy Reed and went all the way with it. I sang with her a couple of times." A July 20, 1961 Fred McDarrah photo shows Neil, Dalton, Mark Spoelstra, and Dylan on harmonica sharing the Café Wha? stage. Fred Neil's verdict: "She sure can sing the shit out of the blues." Nick Cave calls her his favorite female blues singer. She'd been tagged "the folk singer's answer to Billie Holiday" — a comparison she loathed, insisting Bessie Smith mattered more.

The two records are the whole argument. It's So Hard to Tell Who's Going to Love You the Best (Capitol, 1969): producer Nick Venet could not get her to sing until he and Fred Neil convinced her the tape wasn't rolling; most tracks, one take, all in one night at the Record Plant. In My Own Time (1971): recorded at Bearsville Studios (built by Dylan's manager Albert Grossman), produced by Harvey Brooks — who had played bass on Highway 61 Revisited — with Dalton fetching her two teenage kids, her dog, and reputedly her horse from Oklahoma to feel safe enough to record. The room was a Woodstock-session supergroup: Amos Garrett on guitar, pedal-steel pioneer Bill Keith, Denny Seiwell (later Wings' drummer), and John Simon — producer of The Band's Music from Big Pink — on piano.

The deep web: Richard Manuel of The Band wrote "In a Station" specifically for her; The Band's "Katie's Been Gone" on The Basement Tapes is widely said to be about her; Fred Neil's cabin in Saugerties sat on the same road as Big Pink. On the folk side, "Same Old Man" was arranged by Steve Weber of the Holy Modal Rounders, whose bandmate Peter Stampfel wrote the debut's reissue liner notes — the same Rounders orbit as Michael Hurley, a quiet nod back to this series' Snock's week. The inheritors are equally wired: Cat Power's The Covers Record (2000) reaches for Smog's Bill Callahan ("Red Apples") and Michael Hurley ("Sweedeedee") on the same all-covers record that dives into folk-blues tradition; and in 2022, Light in the Attic released Angel Olsen's cover of "Something on Your Mind" as a 7" for In My Own Time's 50th anniversary, with Dalton's original on the B-side. The 2020 documentary Karen Dalton: In My Own Time gave her the screen biography; the 2015 tribute Remembering Mountains set her unpublished notebook lyrics to music (Patty Griffin, Lucinda Williams, Sharon Van Etten, Julia Holter).

The playlist runs as a three-act arc: the Village scene (Dylan, Neil, Hardin) → the two impossible records → the 21st-century inheritors. Eighteen tracks, all original recordings. Dylan's "Moonshiner" is the studio take of the old drinking song he sang at the Gaslight in October 1962 — the dark-side repertoire Dalton and Neil were working two blocks away. Twelve Dalton deep cuts follow (her entire catalog is deep cuts — she never wrote a line). Then the closing trio makes the case for why she matters now: Chan Marshall covering Callahan and Hurley, and Angel Olsen singing the song that anchors the whole revival, 29 years after Dalton's death.
